objectives: Explain personal + subject-matter jurisdiction from Pennoyer to International Shoe.
Walk through pleadings, discovery, + summary judgment under the FRCP.

slides.title: Jurisdiction: personal, subject-matter, + venue
slides.body:
Every civil suit begins with a jurisdictional question: **does this court have power over this defendant + this dispute?** Without jurisdiction, the judgment is void + collaterally attackable. Three doctrines:

**Personal jurisdiction** — power over the defendant:
- **Pennoyer v. Neff (1878)** — Field — territorialist origin: a state has personal jurisdiction over persons + property *within* its borders, full stop. Service of process must be made within the state, or in rem on in-state property. Workable in 1878 horse-+-buggy America; useless for a modern interstate economy.
- **International Shoe Co. v. Washington (1945)** — Stone — paradigm shift. A nonresident defendant is subject to suit if it has **minimum contacts** with the forum state + the suit does not offend **'traditional notions of fair play + substantial justice.'** Replaces Pennoyer's territorialism with a contacts-based inquiry. International Shoe is the most important civil procedure case ever decided.
- **General vs specific jurisdiction**:
  - **General (all-purpose)** jurisdiction: defendant is **'at home'** in the forum (domicile for individuals; place of incorporation + principal place of business for corporations — *Daimler AG v. Bauman* 2014; *Goodyear* 2011). Permits suit on any claim, related or not.
  - **Specific (case-linked)** jurisdiction: defendant's forum contacts give rise to or relate to the claim (*Bristol-Myers Squibb v. Superior Court* 2017; *Ford Motor v. Montana Eighth Judicial District* 2021).
- **Tag jurisdiction (transient/physical presence)**: **Burnham v. Superior Court (1990)** — Scalia plurality + Brennan plurality both upheld personal service while temporarily in California as constitutional personal jurisdiction. **Pennoyer's** territorial principle survives for individuals served in the state.
- **Consent + waiver**: forum-selection clauses (*Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute* 1991); voluntary appearance.
- **In rem + quasi in rem**: jurisdiction over property; modernized in **Shaffer v. Heitner (1977)** — must also satisfy minimum-contacts test.
- **Long-arm statutes**: state statutes that extend jurisdiction to the constitutional limit; specific provisions on tortious acts, transacting business, ownership of property, etc.
- **Purposeful availment + foreseeability**: *World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson* (1980) — Oklahoma cannot exercise specific jurisdiction over a New York Audi dealer merely because a car ended up there. *Asahi Metal v. Superior Court* (1987) — stream of commerce + plus-factors. *J. McIntyre Machinery v. Nicastro* (2011) — plurality on stream-of-commerce + targeting.
- **Personal jurisdiction over Internet defendants**: *Zippo Manufacturing v. Zippo Dot Com* (1997) sliding scale; modern doctrine emphasizes targeted activity rather than mere passive availability.

**Subject-matter jurisdiction** — power over the *case*:
- **Federal-question jurisdiction**: 28 U.S.C. § 1331 — civil actions arising under federal law. *Louisville & Nashville R.R. v. Mottley* (1908) — **well-pleaded complaint rule**: the federal question must appear on the face of the plaintiff's complaint, not in anticipated defenses.
- **Diversity jurisdiction**: 28 U.S.C. § 1332 — citizens of different states + amount in controversy > $75,000. **Complete diversity** required (*Strawbridge v. Curtiss* 1806; Marshall).
- **Supplemental jurisdiction**: 28 U.S.C. § 1367 — codifying *United Mine Workers v. Gibbs* (1966).
- **Removal**: 28 U.S.C. § 1441 — defendants may remove to federal court if original federal jurisdiction.
- **State courts** have **general jurisdiction** (default); federal courts have **limited jurisdiction** (must affirmatively show source).
- **Constitutional grant + statutory grant** must both be present (Article III + statute).

**Venue** — proper district within the system: 28 U.S.C. § 1391 — where defendants reside + where claim arose. **Transfer** (§ 1404 for convenience; § 1406 for cure). **Forum non conveniens** for non-US alternatives (*Piper Aircraft v. Reyno* 1981).

**Erie doctrine** — *Erie R.R. v. Tompkins* (1938) — overruled *Swift v. Tyson*; federal courts sitting in diversity apply **state substantive law** + federal procedural law. *Hanna v. Plumer* (1965) — twin aims of *Erie*: discourage forum-shopping + avoid inequitable administration. *Klaxon Co. v. Stentor* (1941) — federal court applies the choice-of-law rules of the state in which it sits.

Jurisdictional doctrine is technical but foundational: a brilliant lawsuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction yields nothing.

slides.title: Pleadings, discovery, + summary judgment under the FRCP
slides.body:
The **Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (FRCP)**, promulgated in 1938 under the Rules Enabling Act of 1934, transformed federal litigation from technical code pleading into 'notice pleading' + a uniform procedural framework. Chief drafter Charles E. Clark (later 2d Cir.); Edson Sunderland on discovery; Edmund Morgan on evidence. The 1938 Rules were transformative; many states followed suit (California, New York, etc., retain distinct codes). The Rules are amended through the Judicial Conference + Supreme Court + Congress under §2074.

**Pleadings (Rules 7-16)**:
- **Rule 8** — short + plain statement of the claim; **notice pleading**.
- **Rule 9** — heightened pleading for fraud + mistake (with particularity).
- **Rule 10** — form of pleadings.
- **Rule 11** — sanctions against frivolous filings; reasonable inquiry + nonfrivolous arguments.
- **Rule 12** — defenses + motions to dismiss; lack of jurisdiction; failure to state a claim; failure to join party; etc.
- **Rule 15** — amendments + relation back.
- **Twombly + Iqbal** — **Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly (2007)** + **Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009)** — replaced *Conley v. Gibson*'s ('no set of facts') notice-pleading standard with **plausibility pleading**: the complaint must allege facts plausibly suggesting an entitlement to relief; conclusory allegations + legal conclusions disregarded; nonconclusory facts assessed for plausibility. The most consequential procedural change in modern federal civil practice. Massive practical impact on civil-rights, antitrust, employment, securities litigation.

**Discovery (Rules 26-37)**:
- **Rule 26** — general provisions: scope ('relevant to any party's claim or defense + proportional to the needs of the case' — 2015 amendment); initial disclosures (1993 + 2000 amendments); experts; protective orders.
- **Rule 30** — depositions on oral examination.
- **Rule 31** — depositions by written questions.
- **Rule 33** — interrogatories.
- **Rule 34** — production of documents + ESI (electronically stored information); a major battleground.
- **Rule 35** — physical + mental examinations.
- **Rule 36** — requests for admission.
- **Rule 37** — sanctions for discovery abuse; spoliation; Zubulake/Pension Committee/Sekisui line of cases.
- **Privileges + protections**: attorney-client privilege; work-product doctrine (*Hickman v. Taylor* 1947); common-interest privilege.
- **ESI + ediscovery**: predictive coding (*Da Silva Moore* 2012), technology-assisted review, FRE 502, retention policies.

**Pretrial motions**:
- **Rule 12(b)(6)** — motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim (Twombly-Iqbal plausibility).
- **Rule 12(c)** — judgment on the pleadings.
- **Rule 56** — summary judgment. **No genuine dispute of material fact + movant entitled to judgment as a matter of law.**

**The summary-judgment trilogy (1986)** — three Supreme Court cases that transformed summary-judgment practice + made it a routine + decisive procedural mechanism rather than a rare event:
- **Celotex Corp. v. Catrett (1986)** — Rehnquist — movant need not negate the nonmovant's claim; need only **show absence of evidence** to support an essential element on which the nonmovant bears the burden of proof. Shifts the practical burden onto the nonmovant to put forward evidence.
- **Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. (1986)** — White — the substantive **standard of proof** at trial (here, *New York Times v. Sullivan*'s clear-+-convincing actual malice) governs at summary judgment; court asks whether a reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant under that standard. Heightened standards of proof tilt summary judgment toward defendants.
- **Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp. (1986)** — antitrust conspiracy claim; the nonmovant must show 'more than... metaphysically possible' inference; if the inference is implausible, must come forward with more persuasive evidence.

After the trilogy, summary judgment became a **routine dispositive vehicle** + the central battleground of modern civil litigation. ~70% of federal civil cases that reach this stage are decided here rather than at trial. Critics: it has converted a trial right (Seventh Amendment) into a paper exercise.

**Settlement + ADR**: the vast majority of federal civil cases end in **settlement** (~95%); only ~1-3% reach trial. **Mediation** + **arbitration** are widely used (binding arbitration governed by the **Federal Arbitration Act 1925**; *AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion* 2011; *Epic Systems v. Lewis* 2018 — class-action waivers enforceable). The 'vanishing trial' is one of the most significant procedural developments of the late 20th + early 21st centuries (Galanter, 2004).

slides.title: Trial, appeals, class actions, + MDL
slides.body:
**Trial** — only ~1-3% of federal civil cases reach trial. When they do:
- **Jury trial right**: **Seventh Amendment** preserves jury trial in 'suits at common law' over $20; equitable claims (injunctions, specific performance) historically bench-tried. Modern courts use the historical test (*Tull v. United States* 1987; *Granfinanciera v. Nordberg* 1989; *Markman v. Westview* 1996 — patent claim construction is for the court).
- **Voir dire + jury selection**; *Batson v. Kentucky* (1986) + civil extension *Edmonson v. Leesville Concrete* (1991) — equal-protection limits on peremptory challenges by race.
- **Burden of proof**: **preponderance of the evidence** (>50%) in civil; **clear + convincing** in some claims (fraud, defamation by public figures); **beyond a reasonable doubt** is criminal.
- **Bench trials**: Rule 52 — findings of fact + conclusions of law.
- **Judgment as a matter of law** (Rule 50) — formerly directed verdict + JNOV.
- **Jury instructions**, special verdicts, general verdicts with interrogatories.

**Appeals**:
- **Final-judgment rule**: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 — appellate jurisdiction over final decisions only. **Cohen collateral order doctrine** (*Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.* 1949); **interlocutory appeals** (§ 1292(b); class certification under FRCP 23(f); injunctions).
- **Standard of review** — the central appellate doctrine:
  - **De novo** — questions of law; no deference to trial court. Issues like statutory interpretation, motion-to-dismiss grants, summary-judgment grants.
  - **Clearly erroneous** — findings of fact in bench trials (Rule 52(a)(6)); a finding is clearly erroneous when 'the reviewing court on the entire evidence is left with the definite + firm conviction that a mistake has been committed' (*United States v. United States Gypsum Co.* 1948).
  - **Substantial evidence** — agency factual findings + jury verdicts (Rule 50 review).
  - **Abuse of discretion** — discretionary rulings: evidentiary admissibility, scheduling, sanctions, discovery, class certification, equitable relief. Highly deferential.
  - **Harmless error** — even if there was error, reverse only if it affected substantial rights (Rule 61; *Kotteakos v. United States* 1946).
- **Briefs** + **oral argument** + **disposition** (affirm, reverse, remand, dismiss).
- **En banc rehearing** + **Supreme Court certiorari** (Rule 10 — important federal questions, conflicts among circuits, manifest error).

**Class actions — FRCP Rule 23**:
- **Rule 23(a) prerequisites**: numerosity, commonality, typicality, adequacy of representation.
- **Rule 23(b)(1)** — risk of inconsistent adjudications + impairment of nonparty interests.
- **Rule 23(b)(2)** — declaratory + injunctive relief class (civil-rights cases — *Brown v. Board* was effectively this kind of class).
- **Rule 23(b)(3)** — damages class with **predominance + superiority** requirements; the workhorse of consumer + securities + antitrust litigation.
- **Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes (2011)** — Scalia — tightened commonality (must depend on common questions whose answer resolves class claims in one stroke). Largest sex-discrimination class in history dismissed.
- **Amchem Products v. Windsor (1997)** + **Ortiz v. Fibreboard (1999)** — limited settlement classes (asbestos).
- **Comcast Corp. v. Behrend (2013)** — damages model must measure damages attributable to common theory.
- **Tyson Foods v. Bouaphakeo (2016)** — statistical proof to establish classwide liability + damages.
- **CAFA — Class Action Fairness Act (2005)** — expanded federal diversity jurisdiction over class actions to limit forum-shopping into state courts.

**Multi-District Litigation (MDL) — 28 U.S.C. § 1407**:
- The **Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation (JPML)** consolidates federal cases with common questions of fact for pretrial proceedings before a single judge; cases return to their transferor courts for trial unless settled or otherwise resolved.
- Major modern MDLs: opioids (N.D. Ohio Judge Polster); NFL concussion (E.D. Pa.); BP Deepwater Horizon (E.D. La.); 9/11 victim compensation; talc / J&J; 3M earplugs (largest in MDL history by case count); Camp Lejeune. Roughly **40% of all federal civil cases** are in MDLs at any given time.
- Bellwether trials; settlement structures (matrix settlements; common-benefit funds; class settlements within an MDL).

**Complex litigation**: derivative actions (Rule 23.1); interpleader (Rule 22; statutory § 1335); intervention (Rule 24); joinder (Rules 13-21); third-party practice (Rule 14); offer of judgment (Rule 68).

Federal civil procedure rewards strategic foresight: pleadings shape discovery, discovery shapes summary judgment, summary judgment determines whether a trial happens. The lawyer who understands the procedural architecture controls the dispute even before reaching the merits.

question.question: Apply personal-jurisdiction doctrine to a modern e-commerce defendant
question.goal: An Arizona resident sues a Texas-headquartered Internet retailer in Arizona federal court for a defective product purchased online + shipped to Arizona. The retailer ships to all 50 states, advertises nationally, but has no physical presence in Arizona. Analyze personal jurisdiction.

steps.prompt: Is general jurisdiction available in Arizona over the Texas retailer?

acceptedAnswers: No — under Daimler v Bauman (2014) + Goodyear (2011) general jurisdiction lies only where corp is 'at home' (place of incorporation + principal place of business), here Texas — not Arizona

steps.reveal: **Daimler AG v. Bauman (2014)** + **Goodyear Dunlop Tires v. Brown (2011)** confined general jurisdiction to places where the corporation is **'essentially at home'** — paradigmatically place of incorporation + principal place of business. Texas, not Arizona. No general jurisdiction here.

acceptedAnswers: Likely yes — under International Shoe minimum contacts + Ford v Montana (2021) the claim arises from or relates to defendant's contacts with the forum (shipping into Arizona)

steps.reveal: **International Shoe (1945)** — minimum contacts + fair play + substantial justice. **Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District (2021)** — the claim 'arises out of or relates to' the defendant's forum contacts (shipping vehicles into the state, advertising). Here the retailer shipped the product to Arizona; the claim relates to that contact; specific jurisdiction is appropriate.

steps.prompt: What about World-Wide Volkswagen + the stream-of-commerce concerns?

acceptedAnswers: WWVW (1980) prohibited jurisdiction based merely on foreseeable consumer movement; here defendant purposefully targeted Arizona by accepting orders + shipping there

hints: Purposeful availment vs unilateral consumer activity.
steps.reveal: **World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson (1980)** — mere foreseeability of consumer movement into a state is insufficient. But here the retailer **purposefully directed activity** at Arizona — accepted online orders, shipped, advertised. Purposeful availment is satisfied (contrast a passive seller in *J. McIntyre Machinery v. Nicastro* 2011 + the Asahi stream-of-commerce-plus debate). Specific jurisdiction proper.

acceptedAnswers: Subject matter: diversity (28 USC §1332) if amount > $75k + complete diversity; venue: 28 USC §1391 — district where defendant resides or claim arose, here Arizona is fine

steps.reveal: **Subject-matter jurisdiction**: 28 U.S.C. § 1332 — diversity (AZ plaintiff, TX defendant) + amount in controversy > $75k. **Venue**: 28 U.S.C. § 1391 — judicial district where a substantial part of the events occurred (Arizona). Federal removal not at issue since plaintiff filed in federal court. Add **personal jurisdiction** + **subject-matter jurisdiction** + **venue** + **service of process** + you've covered the jurisdictional architecture.

question.question: Why is the 1986 summary-judgment trilogy (Celotex, Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Matsushita) considered transformative for federal civil litigation?
options: **Celotex Corp. v. Catrett (1986)** — Rehnquist — held that a summary-judgment movant need not affirmatively negate the nonmovant's claim; it suffices to point to the **absence of evidence** for an essential element on which the nonmovant bears the burden. **Anderson v. Liberty Lobby (1986)** — White — held that the trial-level **standard of proof** governs at summary judgment; for a public-figure defamation plaintiff (under **New York Times v. Sullivan**), the question is whether a reasonable jury could find clear + convincing evidence of actual malice — heightening the practical bar. **Matsushita Electric v. Zenith Radio (1986)** — antitrust conspiracy theory implausible; nonmovant must come forward with more than 'metaphysically possible' inferences. Together the trilogy converted summary judgment from a **rare device** for clearly meritless claims into a **routine dispositive vehicle** that decides perhaps 70% of cases reaching that stage — the central battleground of modern civil litigation. Critics: this has converted the Seventh Amendment jury-trial right into a paper exercise + advantaged repeat-player defendants with deep document records over individual plaintiffs.
question.explanation: The 1986 trilogy (Celotex + Anderson + Matsushita) transformed summary judgment from rare to routine — the central pretrial dispositive vehicle. Celotex shifted the practical burden; Anderson imposed trial-level proof standards at SJ; Matsushita disciplined implausible inferences. ~70% of cases reaching this stage now decided here.

slides.workedSolution: 1986 summary-judgment trilogy: Celotex (movant points to absence of evidence; burden shifts to nonmovant); Anderson v. Liberty Lobby (trial-level proof standard applies); Matsushita (more than metaphysically possible inferences required). Together they made SJ routine + dispositive; ~70% of federal cases reaching this stage decided here.

question.question: Manage a complex multi-state product liability case
question.prompt: You represent the lead plaintiff in a defective-medical-device case. Thousands of patients across all 50 states have similar injuries. (a) Should you file a **Rule 23 class action** or use **MDL § 1407 consolidation**? Compare the strategic + procedural implications. (b) After **Twombly + Iqbal**, what specific facts must your complaint plead to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss in the modern plausibility regime? (c) Discovery: how would you use Rule 26 + Rule 34 + ESI protocols + technology-assisted review to manage millions of documents from the manufacturer? (d) Apply **Celotex + Anderson** + **Matsushita** to predict how summary judgment will turn on the strength of your causation evidence + expert testimony (*Daubert*). (e) If you certify a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class, address Wal-Mart v. Dukes + Comcast v. Behrend + Tyson v. Bouaphakeo on commonality + damages-model issues.

question.question: Federal diversity jurisdiction requires (a) complete diversity of citizenship and (b) amount in controversy exceeding what threshold (in dollars; 28 U.S.C. § 1332)?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the architecture of a modern federal civil case from filing to final appeal.
question.rubric: Mentions: **Personal jurisdiction** (**International Shoe** 1945; **Pennoyer** 1878 territorial origin; **Burnham** 1990 tag; **Daimler** + **Goodyear** general jurisdiction at home; **Ford v Montana** 2021 specific jurisdiction relates-to). **Subject-matter jurisdiction**: §1331 federal-question + §1332 diversity (>$75k + complete). **Venue** §1391. **Erie doctrine** state substantive + federal procedural in diversity. **Pleadings** under FRCP Rule 8 + **Twombly + Iqbal** plausibility. **Discovery** Rules 26-37 + ESI + ediscovery. **Summary judgment** Rule 56 + 1986 trilogy (**Celotex** + **Anderson v Liberty Lobby** + **Matsushita**). **Trial** — Seventh Amendment jury; preponderance/clear + convincing/beyond reasonable doubt. **Appeals** standards: **de novo** (law); **clearly erroneous** (bench facts); **abuse of discretion** (discretionary). **Class actions Rule 23** (Wal-Mart v Dukes); **MDL §1407** (opioids, 3M, talc). The lawyer who controls the procedural architecture controls the dispute. Concludes: ~95% settle; only ~1-3% reach trial.
